Article Title: Kroger, one of America's oldest grocery chain to layoff thousands; largest in its 143-year history, here's what CEO told employees at townhall
Article Text:
What CEO Greg Foran told employees at townhall

Albertsons wants Kroger to pay $9 billion over failed Kroger deal

America's oldest retail chain Kroger Co plans to eliminate roughly 3,000 corporate positions over the next three years, marking a sweeping workforce reduction as new Chief Executive Officer Greg Foran moves to overhaul the grocer’s management structure. The cuts represent more than one-third of Kroger’s approximately 8,200 corporate staff, making the restructuring one of the largest corporate employees' reductions in the supermarket chain’s 143-year history.Foran, a former Walmart executive, who joined the retailer in February this year, detailed the turnaround strategy in a memo to employees following a companywide meeting on Monday, October 12. The restructuring comes as America's largest traditional grocer contends with slowing top-line growth, fierce retail competition, and persistent inflationary pressures impacting consumer spending. The memo outlined plans to eliminate redundant functions across departments while modernizing daily operations. Kroger is increasingly turning to emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to automate workflows and drive efficiencies across its corporate network.The Cincinnati-based grocery giant announced the layoffs to its employees during an all-company call Monday, October 12. In the memo sent to Kroger employees obtained by the Business Courier, CEO Greg Foran wrote that the company’s transformation will result in the company reducing its corporate workforce across multiple functions by about 3,000 roles.The moves would take Kroger from having about 8,200 corporate workforce employees to roughly 5,200.“As a company, we have made great progress on many fronts with our customers. We started reducing prices and improving our customer experience in stores and online, and we made investments in simplifying our associates’ lives through technology,” Foran wrote. “Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive. We are working to be more agile; more precise in our execution; and deliver benefits to our customers, associates and our shareholders. ”CEO Foran reportedly said that the changes are intended to reduce duplicative work, lower prices and redirect investment toward store employees as the grocer integrates AI into workflows. Kroger expects to start sharing details about the affected roles in the coming months. The reductions will help the company put more resources toward cutting prices, improving shopping experience and investing in frontline employees, Foran wrote in the memo.Foran, who helped turn around Walmart’s US business in the mid- to late 2010s, is implementing Kroger’s biggest price cuts in years, while making service in stores friendlier and faster. The operator of Fred Meyer and Ralphs chains is also taking a more aggressive approach toward supplier negotiations. The company laid off nearly 1,000 corporate employees last year to cut costs.The three-year downsizing marks the latest decisive shift under Foran's leadership as Kroger works to defend its market share against deep-discount rivals and major big-box retailers.Incidentally, the layoffs come at the same time when rival grocery chain Albertsons Cos is demanding that Kroger Co pay more than $9 billion for the collapse of the largest US grocery chain merger in history. Albertsons claims Kroger "willfully breached" its contractual commitments and should pay more than $9.3 billion, including a premium stockholders would have gotten and a $600 million termination fee.
Article Summary: Kroger Co plans to eliminate roughly 3,000 corporate positions over the next three years. The cuts represent more than one-third of Kroger’s approximately 8,200 corporate staff, making the restructuring one of the largest corporate employees' reductions in the supermarket chain's 143-year history. Kroger expects to start sharing details about the affected roles in the coming months.

Article Title: Silicon Valley is facing a 'huge shortage' that has made Dario Amodei make telephone call to Alexandr Wang, Demis Hassabis 'upset' and Elon Musk partner with the company he openly 'trashed' days befor
Article Text:
Elon Musk publicly reverses his stand on Anthropic, days after slamming it

Anthropic's Dario Amodei knocks at rival Meta's door

A global shortage of raw computing power is upending Silicon Valley, sparking bitter corporate turf wars, sending executives on worldwide scrambles for hardware, and forging improbable alliances between fierce rivals, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ). The fierce bottleneck has become the tech industry's central battleground, reshaping executive suites and imperiling the prospects of up-and-coming startups that cannot secure enough chips to keep pace.According to a WSJ report, the severity of the compute crunch was laid bare inside Google, which spent $2.7 billion in 2024 to rehire pioneering researcher Noam Shazeer to steer key projects like its flagship Gemini models. Despite the enormous price tag, Google failed to guarantee Shazeer the computing capacity he sought. After internal reallocations cut his team’s resources in favor of another initiative, Shazeer departed for rival OpenAI, highlighting an internal environment where researchers frequently quarrel over processing power. The Journal reported that Google co-founder Sergey Brin has at times overridden formal allocation procedures to divert compute to his preferred projects, while DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis has expressed frustration over a lack of resources dedicated to fundamental, long-term research.According to an earlier report in CNBC, "One of the biggest points of friction inside Google is compute." The report added, "Google is investing more than almost any company in the world in data centers, chips and related infrastructure. But capacity remains scarce. Every TPU assigned to training a model, serving a Google product, or fulfilling a contract with a cloud customer reflects a choice among competing priorities. " Claiming sources it further said that frustrations over access to compute can be especially acute when Google announces large infrastructure commitments to competing labs like Anthropic, whose models compete directly with Gemini.The scramble for capacity has driven competitors into surprising pacts, most notably between Anthropic and Elon Musk's xAI. Facing severe infrastructure strain and outages triggered by the runaway popularity of its Claude Code assistant, Anthropic dispatched co-founder Tom Brown to xAI’s offices in Hawthorne, California, in late March to negotiate renting compute directly from Musk’s venture. The talks paved the way for Anthropic to lease over 300 megawatts of computing power through an agreement connected to Musk’s company, a deal valued at up to $45 billion. The alliance bridged an ideological divide between Musk and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. Just days before the partnership, Elon Musk, in a post on X, wrote, ""Your AI hates Whites & Asians, especially Chinese, heterosexuals and men. This is misanthropic and evil," Musk wrote. "Fix it."Amodei also reportedly approached Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang in search of excess capacity. According to the report, "Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also spoke on the phone with Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang earlier this year, attempting to source more computing capacity, according to a person familiar with the matter. Meta debated whether to give chips to Anthropic and ultimately decided not to for now, people familiar with the matter said. "Across the wider tech sector, the hunt for computational power resembles a frantic gold rush. Intermediaries like San Francisco Compute are scouring unconventional sites worldwide to locate usable clusters, finding servers running in places as unusual as a converted chicken coop in rural America or navigating monsoon floods in Manila to source hardware in Taipei. Simultaneously, the market has swung aggressively in favor of suppliers: the hourly cost to rent Nvidia H100 chips on one-year contracts jumped 60 percent over the past year, while cloud providers now routinely demand multiyear leases and massive upfront down payments.
Article Summary: Anthropic's Dario Amodei knocks at rival Meta's door in search of more computing power. Google spent $2.7 billion in 2024 to rehire pioneering researcher Noam Shazeer to steer key projects like its flagship Gemini models. The scramble for capacity has driven competitors into surprising pacts.

Article Title: UK's concrete 'sound mirrors' were built after World War 1 to catch bombers; they were abandoned in 1939 because...
Article Text:
The Denge Sound Mirrors near Greatstone Lakes in Kent, built between 1928 and 1930 to detect enemy aircraft by sound.

Britain built sound mirrors because World War 1 left its coast exposed

Radar arrived before the sound mirrors could be perfected

Long before radar screens tracked enemy planes, Britain tried to hear them coming. Three giant concrete structures on the Kent coast, known as the Denge Sound Mirrors, were built between 1928 and 1930 to pick up the drone of approaching aircraft and give the country a few extra minutes of warning. By 1939, they had been abandoned, made obsolete by the arrival of radar.The mirrors still stand near Greatstone Lakes, inside an RSPB nature reserve at Dungeness. From a distance they look like carved stone, but they are made of concrete. Today they draw walkers, photographers and history buffs, and they offer a rare look at how Britain built its early warning systems between the two world wars.The project was led by Dr William Sansome Tucker, a physicist who specialised in acoustics. Britain's coastal towns had suffered heavily from air raids during World War 1, and the government was keen to avoid a repeat. It put serious money into acoustic research that could warn of incoming bombers, and the Denge mirrors were one of the results.Each mirror has a different shape and faces a slightly different direction. Their curved surfaces reflected the sound of aircraft engines onto a focal point, amplifying it enough for operators to pick it up.Depending on which mirror caught the noise, technicians could tell where a threat was coming from and when to scramble fighters.The mirrors had a maximum detection range of about 20 miles. That sounds short today, but aircraft of the late 1920s were slow enough that 20 miles gave defenders time to respond.The first mirror, a 20-foot dish completed in 1928, did not work as intended. Engineers kept refining the design, adding a 30-foot dish and then, in 1930, a 200-foot curved wall that covered a much wider arc of sky. The pace of that iteration was quick for its time.It was not quick enough. Aircraft were getting faster every year, which shrank the warning window, and the mirrors struggled to separate engine noise from wind and other background sounds. When radio-based detection arrived in the late 1930s, it could spot planes far beyond 20 miles, in any weather. The sound mirrors were left to the marshes.They are not the only wartime oddity still standing in England's south. Near Shoreham Airport in Sussex, a graffiti-covered concrete dome once trained anti-aircraft gunners by projecting films of enemy planes onto its ceiling. It was one of 43 such domes built in 1943, and only six survive. The Denge mirrors belong to an earlier chapter of the same story: a country learning, one experiment at a time, how to see what was coming.
Article Summary: Britain built sound mirrors because World War 1 left its coast exposed. The Denge Sound Mirrors were built between 1928 and 1930 to pick up the drone of approaching aircraft and give the country a few extra minutes of warning. By 1939, they had been abandoned, made obsolete by the arrival of radar.

Article Title: Microsoft announces Maia 300, CEO Satya Nadella calls it ‘biggest bet yet on our own silicon’
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls ‘Maia 300’ company’s biggest bet on silicon

Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon.

Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services.

And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems.

We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot.

Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet.

Hardware gains: Density and energy efficiency

Microsoft has announced its third-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip and inference platform, the Maia 300, marking an aggressive push to run more of its AI infrastructure on homegrown hardware after years of heavy reliance on Nvidia’s market-dominant processors. Executive leadership described the rollout as the company’s “biggest bet yet on our own silicon,” positioning the processor as the future operational backbone for its consumer, developer, and enterprise services. Production of the Maia 300 is scheduled to begin in 2027, and Microsoft plans to use the platform as its primary inference engine to process incoming AI queries across its ecosystem, powering tools such as Copilot, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, Foundry and Dragon Copilot.Engineered specifically for complex modern computing, including advanced reasoning, conversational bots and autonomous agentic workflows, the Maia 300 introduces notable efficiency and density leaps over its predecessors.Microsoft plans to install 96 Maia 300 chips into every server rack, effectively doubling the 48-chip density of the Maia 200. The platform achieves up to seven times higher token throughput per rack compared to the Maia 200. Moreover, the hardware is claimed to produce 40% more tokens per megawatt, delivering notable power savings compared to standard GPUs.While Nvidia graphics processing units remain the default industry standard for model training and fill Microsoft’s existing cloud data centers, high market demand and soaring infrastructure costs have pushed major cloud providers toward hardware diversification.Looking ahead, Microsoft plans to scale Azure Maia platforms across multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, according to an announcement from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. General Manager Alistair Speirs declined to provide a more specific timeline for the broader gigawatt expansion, but the trajectory signals Microsoft's clear intent to control its own hardware fate as enterprise AI demand accelerates.
Article Summary: Microsoft has announced its third-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip and inference platform, the Maia 300. Executive leadership described the rollout as the company’s “biggest bet yet on our own silicon,” positioning the processor as the future operational backbone for its consumer, developer, and enterprise services. Microsoft plans to scale Azure Maia platforms across multi- gigawatt deployments starting in 2027.

Article Title: One of the world’s oldest medical journals sends ‘AI-led extinction warning’, says ‘wrong’ use of technology threatens end of humanity in next 75 years
Article Text:
Extinction vectors: AI bioweapons and nuclear famine

AI-engineered biological threats:

Atmospheric nuclear famine:

10% chance AI ‘could kill all humans’ within next decade

In an assessment warning, the Lancet – one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious medical journals – has warned that humanity faces potential extinction by the year 2100, driven by the malicious misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) or the breakout of nuclear conflict, among other reasons. The warning stems from a major findings paper authored by The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, which identified a roster of 17 catastrophic risks capable of undermining human survival and well-being over the next 75 years. Alongside technological hazards and nuclear warfare, the list (via the Guardian) highlights worsening climate breakdown, childhood malnutrition and sharp cuts in foreign aid contributions from wealthy nations.The authors emphasised that these 17 global hazards do not exist in isolation. Because they interact with and amplify one another, international authorities must tackle them collectively. Crucially, the researchers noted that a "realistic route to act" remains viable for every single risk identified.“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” cautioned Professor Christopher Murray, co-chair of the commission and director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington.To rank the severity of emerging hazards, the commission calculated prospective losses in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) – a metric tracking the cumulative years of healthy life lost to chronic illness, permanent disability, or premature death based on current global trends.While the commission calculated that the baseline statistical probability of total human extinction remains low, the absolute consequences of worst-case scenarios could prove irreversible.“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the commission's report warned. The study outlined two primary pathways to complete civilisational collapse:The intentional or rogue use of AI models to design, synthesise and deploy lethal bioweapons.A full-scale atomic exchange injecting sufficient soot and debris into the stratosphere to blot out sunlight, causing a collapse in planetary agriculture and global starvation.In a companion editorial published alongside the core assessment, the journal's editorial team delivered an unsparing verdict:“The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”Recently, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned that AI technology is advancing quickly and he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. He said that the models which currently exist were “low” but he was “worried” the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.
Article Summary: The Lancet has warned that humanity faces potential extinction by the year 2100. The warning stems from a major findings paper authored by The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health. Alongside technological hazards and nuclear warfare, the list highlights worsening climate breakdown, childhood malnutrition and sharp cuts in foreign aid contributions from wealthy nations.

Article Title: Hollywood turns its cameras on Big Tech: Films on Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Facebook’s whistleblower arrive as public worry over AI grows
Article Text:
This image released by Sony Pictures shows writer-director Aaron Sorkin, left, with actor Mikey Madison on the set of "The Social Reckoning." (Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures via AP)

Sony’s The Social Reckoning

Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’

‘You Can See Everything’

Netflix’s ‘Instadocs’ Series

Neon’s ‘Artificial’

Hollywood is brewing a lineup of feature films and documentaries on Silicon Valley this season, tracking some of the most influential and controversial instances in technology and artificial intelligence (AI), just as broader unease over the sector raises. The list includes The Social Reckoning, the scripted drama that serves as a narrative follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s 2010 Oscar-winning The Social Network. Next up is Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’, which Elon Musk criticised for not having integrity. The list also includes ‘Instadocs’ series on Netflix which details the Hugging Face cybersecurity breach, and ‘Artificial’ that recounts OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s firing and return in late 2023.Leading off the lineup this weekend is Sony Pictures’ The Social Reckoning, which is projected to generate roughly $7 million across its domestic opening, as per a report by CNBC. It is a follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network that talked about Mark Zuckerberg’s founding of Facebook, this installment dramatises the events surrounding whistleblower Frances Haugen, who leaked thousands of internal corporate files in 2021.“It brought back really warm memories for me. And so I felt it captured the spirit of that time period,” Haugen told CNBC in a recent interview.Also arriving in limited release this weekend is a nearly four-hour documentary exploring the SpaceX and Tesla chief. While early screenings have earned praise from film critics, Elon Musk lashed out at the production on X, claiming the documentary has zero integrity.Backed by A24 Films and helmed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, this documentary is releasing on October 16 investigates the rise and collapse of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.The streaming platform will premiere an installment detailing the Hugging Face cybersecurity breach, in which a group of rogue OpenAI AI agents slipped past developer controls and testing sandbox to autonomously hack the startup’s backend systems.Coming on Christmas, this is a scripted drama recounting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s high-profile, short-lived firing and return in late 2023. Altman addressed the theatrical project in recent comments to CNBC:“It looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people’s creativity, and I really do support that. I get why people have anxiety. And also if they need to, like, project that anxiety onto someone or have a little bit of relief and poke fun at me, it doesn’t bother me,” Altman said.The cinematic focus arrives alongside growing public apprehension regarding rapid machine intelligence and the physical footprint required to support it. Recent data reveals widespread voter and consumer skepticism with 73% of Americans expressing serious concern about artificial intelligence posing an existential threat to human survival, according to a recent Quinnipiac survey.
Article Summary: Hollywood is brewing a lineup of feature films and documentaries on Silicon Valley this season, tracking some of the most influential and controversial instances in technology. The list includes The Social Reckoning, the scripted drama that serves as a narrative follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s 2010 Oscar-winning The Social Network. Next up is Alex Gibney's ‘Musk’ which Elon Musk criticised for not having integrity.

Article Title: As Elon Musk pushes to expand Starlink across the world, over 11,000 SpaceX satellites that run the network face a growing collision problem in Earth's orbit
Article Text:
Representative Image

Why satellite collisions are becoming a concern for SpaceX

Why some countries do not share satellite data

How international cooperation can help prevent collisions

Starlink satellites are facing a growing collision risk in Earth's orbit. As of 2026, Elon Musk’s SpaceX operates more than 11,000 active Starlink satellites. This makes up a large share of the growing population of spacecraft orbiting Earth. The growing number of satellites and other trackable objects has made collision avoidance challenging for operators, especially as more companies and countries plan to deploy large satellite constellations.To show the scale of the problem, Starlink satellites performed more than 355,000 collision avoidance manoeuvres between May 2025 and May 2026. SpaceX has called for international cooperation to solve this problem, saying that satellite operators sharing data on where their satellites are and where they are heading could help them predict potential collisions and steer more safely around each other in orbit.Earth's orbit contains more than satellites. In 2025, NASA reported tracking over 45,000 man-made objects around the planet, including defunct spacecraft and debris. As satellite networks expand, operators need to track active satellites and objects that could threaten their missions.The challenge is particularly relevant to Starlink, which continues to expand its satellite internet network worldwide.Each additional spacecraft increases the number of objects to monitor, and repeated avoidance manoeuvres can complicate satellite operations.SpaceX has proposed sharing more ephemeris data, which describes a satellite's position, velocity, and trajectory. The company already publishes this information for its own Starlink satellites, but other operators do not consistently make similar data available.At the 2026 International Astronautical Congress in Turkey, Michael Nicolls, SpaceX's vice president for Starlink and president of AI at SpaceXSI, presented information highlighting differences in data-sharing practices among satellite operators.According to the presentation, some organisations in China and Russia were reluctant to share ephemeris data. Some operators in the US, Europe and Japan also did not share the information. Political tensions, national security concerns, and restrictions on sensitive data may explain these differences, although the reasons vary between organisations.Without reliable information about other satellites' movements, operators may struggle to coordinate avoidance manoeuvres, especially when several spacecraft approach the same orbital area.Countries have collaborated in the past to lower the risk of satellite collisions. China and NASA reportedly worked together to avoid a possible satellite collision in October 2025. But the conversation was restricted to information pertinent to that situation.Cooperation could become more important as other companies develop large satellite networks. China's SpaceSail, for example, has plans for a constellation of thousands of satellites that could add to the number of spacecraft operating in low Earth orbit.SpaceX is also developing tools to improve orbital awareness. Its Stargaze system uses observations from Starlink satellites to help identify and track objects that could pose collision risks. Better tracking could support safer operations for multiple satellite operators and help monitor space debris.As satellite constellations continue to grow, avoiding collisions will depend not only on tracking technology but also on how effectively operators exchange information.
Article Summary: As of 2026, Elon Musk’s SpaceX operates more than 11,000 active Starlink satellites. This makes up a large share of the growing population of spacecraft orbiting Earth. The growing number of satellites and other trackable objects has made collision avoidance challenging. SpaceX has called for international cooperation to solve this problem.
